title: The Wall

jokes.text: Dear God, woman.
jokes.setup: Leslie launches immediately into enthusiastic baby shower planning with three activities listed
jokes.punchline: Ron's exasperated, deeply un-sentimental reaction to baby shower enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Swanson economy of disgust. Three words, perfect character voice, sets the comedic dynamic for the scene. Not groundbreaking but executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I am so excited to plan the baby shower! We're going to have games, decorations, tiny little appetizers shaped like baby carriages...

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie. No. Absolutely not. I will not participate in this feminine celebration ritual. Baby showers are a violation of everything I stand for.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, it's just a party to celebrate the baby.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's a trap. A coordinated assault of pastel colors and forced sentimentality designed to extract emotions from grown men. I'd rather sit alone in a dark room eating breakfast food.

jokes.text: I'm gonna make mine look like an astronaut. What are you doing up there in space, baby?
jokes.setup: Leslie is helping plan a baby shower onesie decorating station
jokes.punchline: She breaks into a baby-voice monologue imagining the decorated onesie as an actual space scenario, completely losing the thread
jokes.explanation: Leslie's enthusiastic tangent into baby-space roleplay is charming and character-specific. The self-interruption 'Ah! So cute!' landing her back in reality works well structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to make an astronaut onesie. Oh my god, oh my god, oh my god! It's going to have a big helmet and little rocket boosters on the feet and—Ben, Ben, look at this! We're going to be the cutest astronauts in the whole universe! I'm going to bedazzle the helmet!

jokes.text: Oh, shoot. Really? I'm gonna have to think of something else.
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests an adorable stroller as a gift; Ron says they already have one
jokes.punchline: Leslie's deflation is immediate and comedically sincere — she genuinely hadn't considered this
jokes.explanation: Mild observational beat — Leslie's over-planning meets basic reality. Functional but not especially distinctive.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ron, is that a baby?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Whose baby is that?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Mine.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, whose baby is that? That would be mine. Guys, get in here! Ron has a baby!
jokes.setup: Normal office scene; Ron appears with an infant no one knew about
jokes.punchline: The revelation is treated as a complete shock — Ron had a baby and told absolutely no one
jokes.explanation: Ron's absolute secrecy about his own child's birth is a perfect extension of his character — privacy as pathology. Leslie's escalating disbelief and the office-wide summoning lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron has a baby! Ron has a baby! Ron has a baby!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I asked you not to—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Everyone! Ron Swanson has a baby!

jokes.text: I'd like to introduce you to my son, John middle name redacted Swanson. John was born some time ago, weighing multiple pounds and several ounces.
jokes.setup: Ron introduces his newborn son to the office
jokes.punchline: Every piece of identifying information is deliberately vague or redacted — 'middle name redacted,' 'some time ago,' 'multiple pounds and several ounces'
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the cold open. 'Middle name redacted' is a stroke of genuine comedic writing — it applies Ron's government/military privacy paranoia to the announcement of his own child. 'Born some time ago, weighing multiple pounds and several ounces' escalates the absurdity perfectly. Only Ron Swanson could deliver this. Highly quotable, character-defining, structurally pristine.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'd like to introduce you all to my son. However, I must warn you that this information is classified. If I tell you his name, I will have to kill you.

jokes.text: Much like his father, he is a fan of silence. Please keep your voices down.
jokes.setup: Ron is presenting his newborn to an excited, noisy office
jokes.punchline: He describes the infant's personality as matching his own anti-social preferences and immediately shushes everyone
jokes.explanation: Ron projecting his own misanthropic traits onto his newborn and then demanding quiet in a celebratory moment is perfectly constructed. The pivot from proud father to crowd control is very Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was born on a farm upstate. My parents were very private people. I don't really like to talk about my childhood.

jokes.text: How am I supposed to keep my voice down when you had your baby, and you didn't tell me that you had your baby?
jokes.setup: Ron asks everyone to keep voices down
jokes.punchline: Leslie's righteous indignation at being kept out of the loop overrides all decorum, and she repeats 'your baby' twice as if she can't process it
jokes.explanation: Leslie's inability to process being excluded from a major life event is very her. The repeated 'your baby' shows genuine shock. Solid character work, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm naming him Ramsett. He's antisocial and withdrawn. He hates people. He looks angry at the world.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, he's a baby. He can't hate people.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Not yet. But he will. He'll learn. I'm going to teach him.

jokes.text: Why would you need to know something like that?
jokes.setup: Leslie is outraged Ron didn't tell her he had his baby
jokes.punchline: Ron's genuine bafflement that anyone would expect this information — as if birth announcements are an absurd social custom
jokes.explanation: Nine words that perfectly encapsulate Ron's worldview. His genuine confusion is the joke — he has no social calculus for why people share news. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, why didn't you tell me about the baby?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I didn't think it was relevant.

jokes.text: I have not even sent Diane a gift. She's just walking around, wondering why I haven't sent her a gift yet.
jokes.setup: Leslie realizes she missed the birth announcement
jokes.punchline: Her immediate pivot to worrying about Diane's perception of her gift-giving — imagining Diane wandering around thinking about the gift gap — is wonderfully self-centered while being Leslie-altruistic
jokes.explanation: The image of Diane 'walking around wondering' is funny because it's so Leslie — projecting her own anxiety onto others. Competent but not sharply constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I forgot to send Diane a wedding gift!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She probably thinks I don't care about her. She's probably telling everyone at work that I'm a terrible friend. Her mom is definitely disappointed in me. Diane's definitely disappointed. Her dog is disappointed.

jokes.text: Should we do something? Just let her tire herself out.
jokes.setup: Leslie is spiraling about the gift
jokes.punchline: Ron advises treating Leslie like an overwrought animal — just wait for her to exhaust herself
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Swanson management advice — delivered with the calm of someone who has deeply studied Leslie's patterns. The framing of Leslie as a creature to outlast is funny and affectionate.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I need to give gifts to everyone at the office. Do you know how many people that is? It's like forty people!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're spiraling. Sit. Good girl. Here's a treat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm not a dog.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's what the dog would say.

jokes.text: Could one of you please stop by the pet store and pick up some fish food for me? When did you get a fish?
jokes.setup: After all the drama of revealing his secret baby, Ron asks a favor
jokes.punchline: The favor is completely mundane and reveals yet another secret — he also apparently has a fish no one knew about
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to the cold open. After the revelation of a secret baby, the kicker is an equally secret fish. The escalating secrecy gag lands hard because it's so perfectly calibrated — we expect something significant; we get fish food. Structure is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I need to buy some fish food.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fish food? Ron, do you have fish?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Several.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Several? How many is several?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've stopped counting after twelve.

jokes.text: I think we should book Orin as a headliner. I think it's a no-brainer. Um, he dislocates his shoulder to the music of Billy Joel. The Pawnee Journal called it, 'Why would anyone do this?'
jokes.setup: Youth committee is booking acts for the unity concert
jokes.punchline: April's sincere advocacy for a performer whose entire act is self-injury to Billy Joel music, with a review that is literally just journalistic bafflement
jokes.explanation: The specificity is perfect — not just 'weird performer' but shoulder dislocation to Billy Joel specifically. And the review being literally 'Why would anyone do this?' in a newspaper is an inspired detail. Very April, very absurdist Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Orin could be our headliner! He does experimental performance art.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: What kind of performance art?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, last week he spent three hours lying in a bathtub fully clothed, screaming about government bureaucracy while covered in mayonnaise.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: What did the newspaper say about it?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: The review just said 'Why?'

jokes.text: It was going to be 15, but then this one guy described himself as 'Jackson Pollock-esque' and I told him that's finger painting for adults and I hate it!
jokes.setup: Craig updates on the 14 local artists signed up for the art tents
jokes.punchline: He disqualified a fifteenth artist for describing himself as 'Jackson Pollock-esque,' with Craig's personal art criticism delivered at full emotional volume
jokes.explanation: Craig's over-the-top emotional reactions are his character signature, and here it's well-deployed. 'Finger painting for adults' is a genuinely good line. The escalation to 'I hate it!' is the Craig payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: We had a signup for the art tent. One guy wanted to display his work. I asked him what kind of art. He said, 'I create installations that challenge the bourgeois construct of reality.' So I told him we don't have room and he should leave.

jokes.text: Pawnee might once again tolerate-slash-ignore me. I know that sounds bad, but for a politician it's pretty much the best-case scenario.
jokes.setup: Leslie confessional about the unity concert being her shot at redemption with the town
jokes.punchline: Her goal is to be 'tolerated-slash-ignored' and she immediately acknowledges this sounds pathetic — then reframes it as political success
jokes.explanation: Sharp political satire embedded in Leslie's confessional. The self-awareness of the joke — she knows it's sad, but contextualizes it as realistic — is both funny and a bit poignant. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm organizing a unity concert to bring the whole town together. My goal is to create an event so inclusive and non-partisan that literally no one can complain about it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: If we can get through one evening without a single person tweeting something negative, I will consider this the greatest political achievement in the history of human civilization.

jokes.text: 'Grant Larson,' otherwise known as Elton John. Congratulations, Leslie.
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she has booked a meeting with 'none other than Grant Larson'
jokes.punchline: A committee member assumes it must be a celebrity alias for Elton John, and congratulates her with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The Elton John assumption is a good misdirect — Leslie's build-up implies something more exciting than a bureaucrat. The deadpan congratulations lands. Moderately clever.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, I know 'tolerance' sounds bad, but in politics, it's actually a huge compliment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It means, 'I don't think you're going to destroy everything.'

jokes.text: He's basically the Liam Bonneville of the Midwest. Liam Bonneville? The department of the interior's resident bad boy? He's basically the Tim Dweck-- Okay, never mind.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to explain who Grant Larson is by referencing more obscure bureaucrats
jokes.punchline: Each reference is a more obscure government official than the last, with 'resident bad boy' for a DOI staffer being the peak absurdity, until she gives up mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: The escalating bureaucratic name-dropping, culminating in 'department of interior's resident bad boy,' is excellent Leslie Knope comedy. The concept of a 'bad boy' at the DOI is inherently funny. Giving up mid-third-reference is a perfect structural choice.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm about to say something that will blow your mind. Are you ready? Because this is big. This is really big. Like, career-defining big.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know how when you're driving down the highway at night, and suddenly you see this massive billboard lit up? And it's so bright and so unexpected that you have to shield your eyes? That's what you just did to my brain. You are that billboard. Except instead of advertising beer or car insurance, you're advertising pure excellence.

jokes.text: And that banner unfurling marks the 100th time that one of my projects has been... ahead of schedule.
jokes.setup: Leslie triumphantly declares the project 'ahead of schedule' and a banner unfurls — but the cut to a new timestamp suggests the banner is comically slow
jokes.punchline: The punchline is split across a scene break: the banner unfurl takes so long that we cut away at [03:13] and come back at the same line, implying the banner took a ridiculous amount of time
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of a banner unfurl taking so long it eats into the next segment is a reliable physical comedy beat. The irony of 'ahead of schedule' being demonstrated by the slowest possible banner is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Grant Larson is basically the Ryan Gosling of municipal government.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, Grant Larson looks nothing like Ryan Gosling.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, not anymore. Ryan Gosling's aged really well.

jokes.text: ...besides the unveiling of Tricia's new highlights. You think I wouldn't notice? You look fly as hell, girl!
jokes.setup: Leslie is declaring the unity concert 'the biggest event of 2014'
jokes.punchline: She breaks from her formal announcement to personally compliment a committee member's hair in the middle of the meeting, completely abandoning professional register
jokes.explanation: Leslie's inability to not be warm and personal even in formal settings is charming and funny. 'You look fly as hell, girl' in the middle of an official announcement is good tonal whiplash.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben is like... like the peanut butter to my jelly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No wait, he's like the Ross to my Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He's like the Mulder to my Scully.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He's like the Moonlight Sonata to my... Moonlight Concerto.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? He's just Ben. I can't explain it.

jokes.text: I'm gonna do what I do best-- lock down deals. And dork-asaurus over here is gonna handle the boring stuff. You said you genuinely valued my business acumen. Also, I'm your boss.
jokes.setup: Tom and Ben introduce their sponsorship meeting roles in a confessional
jokes.punchline: Tom reduces Ben to 'dork-asaurus handling the boring stuff'; Ben's two-part rebuttal — first citing Tom's own compliment, then pulling rank — gets progressively more desperate
jokes.explanation: The double-punchline structure (compliment callback + 'I'm your boss') is solid. 'Dork-asaurus' is a fun Tom insult. Ben's exasperation is character-true. Nothing exceptional but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're here to celebrate an arbitrary milestone. Today marks the 47th consecutive day that I have arrived at work on time.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'd like to thank my alarm clock, my car, and my unwavering commitment to municipal excellence.

jokes.text: Look what Gayle made for the baby. It says 'Property of Pawnee Government.' Isn't that adorable?
jokes.setup: Office staff are fawning over Ron's baby
jokes.punchline: Someone presents a onesie reading 'Property of Pawnee Government' as if it's an adorable gift, not a slightly dystopian statement
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of a government ownership claim on a newborn, presented with total sweetness, works well. The irony is understated and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This unity concert is going to be the biggest event of 2014.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: By the way, your hair looks amazing today.

jokes.text: Today might be the day that I finally crowd surf. I should probably empty my pockets just in case.
jokes.setup: Leslie is excited about the press conference at the park
jokes.punchline: Her excitement escalates to anticipating crowd surfing at a government press conference, and her practical preparation for it underscores her complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The two-part joke lands well — the absurd aspiration (crowd surfing a press conference) made funnier by the mundane practical preparation. Leslie's earnestness is the engine here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, you're being a real Donna right now.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What does that even mean?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't know, but it's not a compliment. You're all up in my business about my responsibilities.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's literally my job. I'm the Deputy Director.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, I'm the Deputy Deputy Director of not caring what you think.

jokes.text: ...in front of a picture of a bald eagle giving the middle finger.
jokes.setup: Leslie discovers the graffiti she thought was painted over has been replaced with new graffiti
jokes.punchline: The new graffiti is specifically a bald eagle flipping the bird — absurd imagery that mixes patriotism with hostility
jokes.explanation: A bald eagle giving the middle finger is a genuinely funny, specific, and visually distinct image. It works both as Pawnee worldbuilding and as an image so specific it demands to be seen. Good economy in how Leslie describes it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You said you valued my business skills.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But the more important fact is that I'm in charge.

jokes.text: Yeah, you probably wanna stand to the side so people can see it.
jokes.setup: Leslie is upset about the bald eagle middle finger graffiti behind the press conference spot
jokes.punchline: Someone earnestly suggests staging the shot so the graffiti is clearly visible — treating the disaster as a production opportunity
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan. Treating Leslie's catastrophe as a framing opportunity is a solid Pawnee-logic joke. Moderate craft.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look at this adorable little onesie I got for the baby! It says 'Department of Parks and Recreation' on it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I had it custom made. I wanted the baby to start learning about proper government organization from day one.

jokes.text: On it, boss. Ahh! Ow. The Kool-Aid Guy makes it look so easy.
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'we should just knock down this wall' and a staffer immediately charges it
jokes.punchline: The staffer slams into the wall and hurts themselves; their recovery line references the Kool-Aid Man as if this was an achievable standard
jokes.explanation: 'The Kool-Aid Guy makes it look so easy' is an excellent recovery line — self-aware, pop-culture-anchored, and delivered from a position of pain. The physical setup is predictable but the specific reference elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to crowd surf at the press conference. Ben, help me practice by throwing me in the air repeatedly.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, no. That's not appropriate for a government announcement.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I've seen it work at concerts. How is this different?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because one involves music and a crowd that wants to be there, and the other involves city officials and a potential lawsuit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're thinking about this all wrong. This is going to blow people's minds.

jokes.text: In the time I've worked here, I've taken great pains to see as little of this building as possible. Turns out the third floor is silent, empty, and completely free of government work. I can't think of anything more beautiful to share with my son.
jokes.setup: Ron confessional explaining why he's brought baby John to the office's abandoned third floor
jokes.punchline: His criteria for 'beautiful' — silence, emptiness, absence of government work — is Ron's entire philosophy compressed into a baby bonding moment
jokes.explanation: Genuinely touching and funny simultaneously. Ron's version of fatherly beauty — sharing a space devoid of government work — is a perfect distillation of his character. The warmth underneath the anti-government grumpiness is what makes Parks work.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Where are you going to stand?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right here by the unity wall.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh no.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You might want to look at it first.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why would I— oh my God!

jokes.text: If I had a toolbox I could take care of that faulty radiator. Ooh! This place is a paradise!
jokes.setup: Ron is discovering the joys of the abandoned third floor
jokes.punchline: A broken radiator inspires tool-lust, and his 'paradise' is a dusty government floor with a plumbing problem
jokes.explanation: Ron's version of paradise involving a broken radiator and the potential to fix it is perfectly character-specific. The exclamation point on 'paradise' over a government utility problem is good comedic deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I spent all weekend removing graffiti from the park. All of it. Every single tag.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's admirable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you, Ron. I really think we can keep it clean if—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Uh, Leslie? There's new graffiti on the bathroom door.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? I just— that was— NO!

jokes.text: You guys make my favorite teeth-whitening strips-- pearlies for girlies. It's unisex. The cartoon princess on the label says so.
jokes.setup: Tom meets Mitch from Savner Bleaches and recognizes the brand
jokes.punchline: Tom calls them 'pearlies for girlies'; Mitch insists they're unisex; the proof is a cartoon princess label — which is itself evidence against the claim
jokes.explanation: The triple-beat structure (name, claim of unisex, proof via princess) is well-constructed. The self-defeating logic of 'it's unisex, says the cartoon princess' is the comedic target and it's hit cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Do you know what I saw today? Someone spray-painted over the American flag mural on Fifth and Main. They turned the eagle into... I can't even say it. It's an obscenity. A bald eagle! Our national bird! Desecrated!

jokes.text: I may have a few eggs ready to hatch in the personal idea nest.
jokes.setup: Mitch invites Tom to pitch business ideas
jokes.punchline: Tom's confident acknowledgment uses a mangled business metaphor — 'eggs ready to hatch in the personal idea nest' — as if this is professional language
jokes.explanation: Tom's business-speak is a reliable comedy mode. 'Personal idea nest' is a funny specific coinage. Not standout but characterful.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is unacceptable. Someone drew an offensive eagle on the community center wall.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why don't you just highlight it? Make it a teaching moment. Add some flowers around it, maybe a inspirational quote.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, that's... actually that might work.

jokes.text: It's all happening, Ben. Soon I'll have a new career, new crib, new friends. If all goes well, this may be one of the last times I ever have to speak to you.
jokes.setup: Tom is excited about the potential investor meeting
jokes.punchline: His excitement escalates to the conclusion that success means never speaking to Ben again — delivered warmly, as if it's a shared aspiration
jokes.explanation: The pivot from ambitious list to 'never speak to you again' is a good punchline structure. Tom's delivery of this as aspirational rather than cruel is the character-specific twist.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh yeah!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, that didn't work.

jokes.text: I was told there'd be a free barbecue buffet? Just take some beef jerky and...hush!
jokes.setup: Leslie thanks people for attending the press conference
jokes.punchline: Someone came only for a promised barbecue; Leslie substitutes beef jerky and tries to silence them
jokes.explanation: Classic Pawnee citizenry — showing up only for food and needing to be managed. The 'beef jerky and hush' solution is a good Leslie improvisation. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Finding paradise is a place without government work.

jokes.text: Bees! Bees! Oh! Nobody panic! Ohhh, noooo! Ah! It stung me in the eyeball!
jokes.setup: Leslie's ceremonial wall demolition begins with great fanfare
jokes.punchline: The wall was full of bees; the Eagletonians swing into the hive and unleash a swarm; chaos erupts including an eyeball sting
jokes.explanation: The bee chaos sequence is primarily visual/physical comedy. 'It stung me in the eyeball' is a great specific escalation. High impact as a set piece even if the setup is fairly standard disaster comedy. The real craft is in what follows.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This product is completely unisex. Look, it comes in purple!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And the cartoon character on the box? Sure, she's got a bow in her hair and long eyelashes, but that doesn't mean it's just for girls.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Guys can wear bows. Guys can have eyelashes. It's 2014, people.

jokes.text: The wall demolition releases a swarm of bees, stinging everyone — mostly Eagletonians
jokes.setup: Leslie has ceremonially given Eagletonians the first strike at the wall as a unity gesture
jokes.punchline: The wall is full of bees; chaos ensues; the Eagletonians who struck it get stung most
jokes.explanation: A strong visual set piece. The situational irony — unity gesture causes immediate injury to one side — is solid plot comedy. The escalating panic ('Bees! Bees! Oh!') is slapstick that works in the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've got ideas for days. I'm like a idea factory, except the factory is also an idea, and the ideas coming out of the factory are ideas about factories that make ideas.

jokes.text: Oh, man, this is amazing, man. The stupid Eagletonians are totally getting pwned by these bees. I'm gonna send this straight to Tosh.
jokes.setup: Bee chaos is unfolding and injuring Eagletonians
jokes.punchline: A Pawneean is delighted and immediately plans to submit the footage to a viral video show — pure schadenfreude
jokes.explanation: Good Pawnee-vs-Eagleton characterization. The Tosh.0 reference is slightly dated but works in context. Functional comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, my man, I need your help with something. You're not smart, but you're like, organized-smart, you know? Like a smart person's filing cabinet.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not a compliment, Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know, but I need you anyway.

jokes.text: Don't worry, babe, I'll protect you. I got stung once, I'm immune. Go ahead and sting me, bees. It does nothing.
jokes.setup: Bee chaos; a man tries to protect his partner
jokes.punchline: His protection strategy is based on the completely false belief that one bee sting grants immunity; he challenges the bees with heroic confidence
jokes.explanation: 'Go ahead and sting me, bees. It does nothing.' is a great line — the confident misunderstanding of bee biology combined with the heroic challenge is very funny. Good escalation within the bee chaos.

dialogue.speaker: City Council Member
dialogue.line: Where's the food you promised us?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh! Yes, about that. I have some complimentary packets of Equal and a half-empty jar of garlic powder. You're welcome.

dialogue.speaker: City Council Member
dialogue.line: That's not food.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's a condiment situation. Work with me here. Meeting adjourned!

jokes.text: Leslie, it appears that most of the people that were stung were from Eagleton. How did you pull that off?
jokes.setup: The bee disaster has selectively hit Eagletonians because they were closest to the wall
jokes.punchline: A reporter assumes this is an elaborate Pawnee prank and congratulates Leslie on her precision bee-targeting
jokes.explanation: The reporter's conspiratorial 'how did you pull that off?' treats obvious chaos as a masterful prank. Good inversion. The follow-up exchanges build this well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Everyone, please remain calm. The wall breaking ceremony is proceeding exactly as planned.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Leslie, there are bees everywhere!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Those weren't on the schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I specifically requested a bee-free zone.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: This is the best day ever.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Treat yo self... to a bee sting! No, that doesn't work!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: I'm allergic! Why is this happening to me?

jokes.text: They were not my bees, Trodd. And for the last time this was not a prank. I mean, in fact you should treat this like a public service announcement. Everybody...should check their walls for bees.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to explain the bees were not intentional
jokes.punchline: Her pivot to a public service announcement — 'everybody should check their walls for bees' — is Leslie's crisis management at its most absurd-logical
jokes.explanation: 'Everybody should check their walls for bees' is a very quotable line — Leslie trying to spin a disaster into a civic message is classic. The 'in fact' pivot is perfectly structured.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnee Resident
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! Someone get this on video! This is going to be huge on TikTok!

jokes.text: Nice try, prank queen. Probably bees in there.
jokes.setup: Leslie insists the bees were not a prank
jokes.punchline: The reporter has fully committed to the prank theory and now sees hidden bees as part of an ongoing conspiracy
jokes.explanation: 'Prank queen' is a funny title and 'probably bees in there' as a catchphrase paranoia is good escalation of the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I've been stung by bees before. I'm immune now.

dialogue.speaker: Girlfriend
dialogue.line: That's not how immunity works.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.line: Sure it is. I got stung last summer, and I didn't die. So now my body knows how to handle it.

dialogue.speaker: Girlfriend
dialogue.line: You're going to get us both killed.

jokes.text: Larry, just tell him I need to reschedule because I am trying to fix my bee hole disaster. Wait! No, wait! No! Larry, don't tell him that. Don't mention my bee hole.
jokes.setup: Leslie gets a call from a major contact during the bee crisis
jokes.punchline: She instructs Larry to explain using the phrase 'bee hole disaster' and then desperately tries to unsay it — 'don't mention my bee hole'
jokes.explanation: 'Don't mention my bee hole' is the best single line of the episode. The two-stage structure — she says it, then realizes and tries to retract it — is perfectly constructed. 'Bee hole' works as both a literal description and an inadvertent double entendre. Highly quotable, absurd yet earned. The moment is made funnier by how Leslie immediately recognizes the problem but it's too late.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The one Pawnee resident who got stung? Ben Wyatt. Poetic justice.

jokes.text: We're gonna be kinda loud. My son is several weeks old. He's quite familiar with the sound of power tools.
jokes.setup: A construction crew warns Ron that their work will be noisy
jokes.punchline: Ron's response — that his infant is already power-tool-familiar — implies he's been workshop parenting since birth, as if this is completely normal
jokes.explanation: 'Several weeks old, quite familiar with the sound of power tools' is a perfect Ron Swanson line. The implication that he's had the infant in the workshop for weeks is funny and entirely believable for this character. Economy and character integration are both high.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: So you're saying you had nothing to do with the bee incident?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's right. I would never prank anyone with bees.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: But you do have bees? Like, a lot of bees?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What? No! Why would I have bees?

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: So the bees everywhere are just a coincidence?

jokes.text: Okay, how about this one-- Lasik for fingernails? Cut your fingernails once, never have to cut 'em again. All we need is a complicated laser I have no idea how to build. Seems impossible.
jokes.setup: Tom is desperately trying to pitch a business idea to Ben before the investor meeting
jokes.punchline: Fingernail Lasik — a procedure that requires a laser Tom explicitly cannot build, acknowledged immediately as impossible
jokes.explanation: The self-defeating business idea pitch is good — Tom articulates the problem himself ('a complicated laser I have no idea how to build') without losing confidence. Ben's flat 'seems impossible' is the perfect straight-man landing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to reschedule the meeting. How about Thursday at 2?

dialogue.speaker: Parks Department Employee
dialogue.line: That doesn't work. I have to inspect the bee hole.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The bee hole? We could do it in the bee hole.

dialogue.speaker: Parks Department Employee
dialogue.line: Um... okay.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, if you're already going to be in the bee hole, we might as well have the meeting there. In the bee hole.

jokes.text: Uh-oh! 'Saltweens!' Saltines for tweens. Seems...unnecessary?
jokes.setup: Tom pitches another business idea
jokes.punchline: Saltines for tweens — a snack that already exists, rebranded for a demographic that doesn't need it — with Ben's perfectly phrased 'seems unnecessary?' as the response
jokes.explanation: 'Saltweens' is a great portmanteau — the name does all the work. Ben's 'seems unnecessary?' with the rising question mark is perfectly calibrated skepticism. Good economy throughout. One of the better quick gags in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'm not worried. My son was exposed to construction noise in the womb. It toughened him up.

jokes.text: Restaurants were ranked number one in Accounting Magazine's 'Riskiest Businesses' issue. That was their last issue before they folded, actually. Magazines are also very risky.
jokes.setup: Ben warns Tom that restaurants are the riskiest business
jokes.punchline: The source of the warning was itself a failed business — the magazine folded — which Ben immediately acknowledges as confirmation of his broader thesis
jokes.explanation: This is excellent joke construction. The self-defeating citation (magazine that folded as source for business failure) is a tight logical loop. 'Magazines are also very risky' as the conclusion is perfectly deadpan and Ben-specific — the guy who would know this fact and feel compelled to note it. Structure is near-perfect with the three beats building logically. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, okay. So I'm thinking we take those fancy MRI machines, right? The ones that cost like two million dollars?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And we turn them into tanning beds. High-tech tanning beds. We call it 'MRI Tan.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: People want to look good AND know what their spleen looks like. It's a win-win.

jokes.text: I can't believe an angel investor floated down from the heavens, and I don't even have anything to pitch him. Come on, you must've had one good business idea. You're 52 years old!
jokes.setup: Tom realizes he has no solid pitch for the investor meeting
jokes.punchline: His desperation leads him to invoke Ben's age (incorrectly) as evidence he must have accumulated business ideas — Ben denies being 52
jokes.explanation: Tom's desperation pivot to ageism is funny but the Ben-is-52 joke is low-investment. Works primarily as a transition beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're targeting an underserved demographic: people who eat crackers. It's a $47 billion industry.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, that's just... everyone eats crackers.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly. We're being very specific about our market.

jokes.text: You would be the middleman between dry cleaners and the companies that sell chemicals to dry cleaners. Wow! Right? You're right, man. That is not sexy.
jokes.setup: Ben reveals his supposedly air-tight business idea
jokes.punchline: The idea is spectacularly mundane — a B2B chemical middleman — and Tom's sincere 'Wow!' followed by immediate deflation is the joke
jokes.explanation: Ben's idea being so boring that even the person pitching it agrees 'that is not sexy' is good character work — this is exactly the idea Ben would have. Tom's genuine 'Wow!' before he processes the content is a nice beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: According to this article in Business Monthly, the top business risks are overexpansion, poor management, and—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh no. Business Monthly just went out of business.

jokes.text: Leslie Knope's little stunt put three people in the hospital. This bee incident is just the latest assault coming from the Pawnee side of this merger. Mike Patterson is Eagleton's most tenacious reporter. When he sinks his teeth into something, he's like a dog with a bone! Oh, my God! You can't lean in to whisper and then yell. That's not fair.
jokes.setup: An Eagleton reporter is doing a dramatic whisper-to-yell delivery for effect
jokes.punchline: Leslie's genuine startled complaint — 'you can't lean in to whisper and then yell, that's not fair' — breaks the fourth wall of interview convention
jokes.explanation: The reporter's theatrical whisper-yell is a recognizable media affectation, and Leslie calling it out as 'not fair' is wonderfully genuine. The specific complaint ('you can't lean in to whisper AND then yell') is both funny and correct. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You should have some solid business ideas by now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm not that old!

jokes.text: It was a prank though, right? So sad. People will believe anything.
jokes.setup: Leslie is lamenting that people think the bee incident was a prank
jokes.punchline: April casually asks if it was actually a prank, then immediately pivots to 'people will believe anything' when Leslie says no — as if she barely cares
jokes.explanation: April's completely casual inquiry about whether the disaster was intentional, followed by non-committed empathy, is very her. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, I've been thinking about getting into the dry cleaning chemical business. It's actually a really underrated industry with huge profit margins.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That sounds... great, man.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You don't sound excited.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, I am. Dry cleaning chemicals. That's... that's the dream.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay. You're right. It's not that exciting.

jokes.text: Who's a big guy?
jokes.setup: Craig is dramatically exiting after his emotional breakdown
jokes.punchline: He pauses to ask 'Who's a big guy?' — apparently self-soothing with the same baby talk one uses on an infant, or seeking validation from colleagues before exiting
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum absurdity. 'Who's a big guy?' as Craig's self-soothing exit line is bizarre and perfect — is he asking others? Himself? It's funnier for being unexplained. Economy is near-perfect. A genuinely weird, memorable character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe that reporter is here. This is huge for Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You just whispered that and now you're yelling.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm excited!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your volume control is like a broken dimmer switch.

jokes.text: I'm sure the government believed you when you told them that, and I tip my cap to you for profiting off their ignoe. But I'm offering you two months paid vacation and the ability to take credit for my work, which will be flawless.
jokes.setup: The construction foreman says this is too much work for one person; Ron offers to do it himself
jokes.punchline: Ron critiques the foreman for government grift ('ignoe' — presumably 'ignorance'), then offers a counter-deal: Ron does all the work, the foreman takes credit and vacation
jokes.explanation: Ron's anti-government critique embedded in a practical negotiation is great character work. Acknowledging the contractor's government-billing scam approvingly before out-offering him is Ron Swanson at his most functional-anarchist. 'Which will be flawless' is quietly very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I don't do well with conflict. Last Thanksgiving, I had to choose between my family and my principles, and let's just say the cops sided with my family.

jokes.text: Now I know what you're thinking. What if it's a cleaner who wants to buy glycol ethers? Ben, stop! This is so boring! This is like listening to a TED talk by the color beige.
jokes.setup: Ben is pitching the dry cleaning chemical middleman idea to Tom with full enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'TED talk by the color beige' simile — the ultimate dull-on-dull metaphor — perfectly captures why this idea is unsellable
jokes.explanation: 'A TED talk by the color beige' is one of the best lines in the episode. The layered metaphor — TED talks are already known for a certain performative earnestness, and beige is the universal signifier of bland — creates a compound image of spectacular dullness. Highly quotable, original phrasing, character-appropriate for Tom. Earns a high score.

dialogue.speaker: Construction Foreman
dialogue.line: This job is going to take six to eight weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why don't you fellas take a break? Relax. I'll do the work.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You can take all the credit.

jokes.text: Well, I sold tons of awesome stuff. Guess it makes sense my next challenge is to sell something mind-numbingly dull. Dull? Does this look dull to you? Ahhhh.
jokes.setup: Tom realizes he might be the right person to sell Ben's boring idea
jokes.punchline: Ben takes offense at 'dull' and responds with some kind of dramatic gesture ('Ahhhh') as if the chemicals are exciting — implying he genuinely doesn't see the problem
jokes.explanation: Ben's indignant defense of his boring idea is good character work. The physical reaction ('Ahhhh') implies some kind of passionate chemical demo that we can only infer from the subtitle. Works better on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Did you know that phosphate pricing has increased 340% in the last five years?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I did know that. Because you told me. While I was being slowly buried alive in a box of dirt.

jokes.text: I'm so incredibly sorry. That's very kind of you, Ms. Knope. I hope you look a lot less gross very soon.
jokes.setup: Leslie visits bee sting victims in the hospital to apologize
jokes.punchline: A victim accepts her apology and reciprocates by wishing she looks 'a lot less gross very soon' — implying Leslie's bee-stung appearance is notable
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — the victim ends up pitying Leslie's appearance. 'A lot less gross' delivered with apparent sincerity is a nice deadpan beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: Did you get a lot of gifts when you were in the hospital?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, I got flowers, balloons, a casserole, get-well cards from half the department.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: That's nice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what you're not getting? Sympathy. Because you've been really cruel to me.

jokes.text: Thanks for coming, Knope. I knew we were besties. What do you got in there for me, some dirty mags? No! These gift baskets are for innocent victims... not for jerks who got stung because they were laughing at other people's pain.
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives at the hospital; Jamm is there and acts like they're close friends
jokes.punchline: Jamm assumes the gift baskets are for him and guesses 'dirty mags'; Leslie clarifies they're for people who deserve them, explicitly excluding Jamm
jokes.explanation: Jamm assuming he's owed dirty magazines is in-character. Leslie's principled exclusion is a good character beat. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Mike Patterson
dialogue.line: Leslie Knope showed up at Ramsett Hospital today, ostensibly to visit an injured constituent. But was she really there to help? Or was she there to exploit this tragedy for her own political gain?

dialogue.speaker: Mike Patterson
dialogue.line: We'll have more on this story as it develops.

jokes.text: Whatever. Got a lotta filth in my kindle anyway. We can just hang.
jokes.setup: Leslie refuses to give Jamm a gift basket
jokes.punchline: Jamm cheerfully pivots to revealing he has 'a lotta filth in his Kindle anyway' and proposes they hang out instead
jokes.explanation: 'A lotta filth in my Kindle anyway' is a characterful line — very Jamm. The casual digital smut-reveal as a social offer is funny and specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why are you wearing a tie-dye shirt?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm using a distraction technique. While everyone's looking at my shirt, I can get work done.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not how that works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, it's working right now because you're distracted by my shirt.

jokes.text: We're live ambushing Leslie Knope who's in the middle of a crass publicity stunt, shoving cameras into the faces of these poor, injured victims. These are your cameras. This is not a publicity stunt. I just came here by myself to apologize.
jokes.setup: Mike Patterson ambushes Leslie with a camera crew at the hospital
jokes.punchline: He accuses her of a publicity stunt with cameras — while using his own cameras to do exactly that — and Leslie's calm rebuttal ('these are your cameras') is the logical counter
jokes.explanation: The media self-contradiction — accusing someone of camera-shoving with your own cameras — is good hypocrisy comedy. Leslie's flat 'these are your cameras' is a sharp counter.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have some good news.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Just kidding. I wanted to give you hope before I crushed it with bad news.

jokes.text: Really? Because all we see is you talking to your friend, known Eagleton hater Jeremy Jamm. Excuse me, Mike. That's, uh, best friend.
jokes.setup: Patterson frames Jamm as 'known Eagleton hater' to make Leslie look bad
jokes.punchline: Jamm interrupts only to correct 'friend' to 'best friend' — completely undermining any defense and happily aligning himself with the worst label
jokes.explanation: Jamm correcting 'friend' to 'best friend' while being called an Eagleton hater is excellent. He hears only the flattery of the relationship label and ignores the damning context. Perfect character work with great economy — seven words do a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, I think of challenges like clouds. They're big and scary, but the sun is always behind them, and eventually they drift away.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's actually just a cloud of bird poop that fell on my windshield this morning.

jokes.text: Awesome idea, Lezzie. As a matter of fact I say we should secede from Eagleton! Whose dumbass idea was it for them to merge anyway? Mine. It was my idea.
jokes.setup: Leslie makes a speech about Pawneeans and Eagletonians coming together; Jamm endorses it
jokes.punchline: Jamm mishears/misunderstands the message as a secession endorsement, advocates it loudly, then Leslie has to claim authorship of the merger he's attacking
jokes.explanation: Jamm's immediate misreading of a unity speech as a secession call, followed by Leslie having to claim the 'dumbass idea' in real time, is good situational comedy. The escalation from Leslie's idealism to immediate chaos is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben! BEN! Why would you give me the wrong materials for my presentation?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I didn't give you anything, Tom. You asked for those yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, can you help me fix this?

jokes.text: You heard it here first. Self-proclaimed dumbass Leslie Knope and councilman Jeremy Jamm are spearheading a Pawnee secession movement.
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'mine, it was my idea' in reference to the merger Jamm called a dumbass idea
jokes.punchline: Patterson immediately packages Leslie's self-defense as a 'self-proclaimed dumbass' moment for broadcast
jokes.explanation: The media spin from Leslie's statement to 'self-proclaimed dumbass' is a good joke about how quotes get weaponized. Quick and well-constructed.

jokes.text: Don't touch my camera, you Pawnee animal! Name-calling, huh? Classy move, douche bag. Oh! All right. Is that how you wanna play? Yeah! Come on! No fighting in a hospital. There shouldn't be fighting in a hospital! Wish I had my ninja stars!
jokes.setup: The hospital situation has devolved into a confrontation between the Pawnee contingent and the Eagleton camera crew
jokes.punchline: Jamm's specific regret — 'wish I had my ninja stars' — is the peak of the escalation; the absurdity of a city councilman owning and routinely carrying ninja stars is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'Wish I had my ninja stars' is a great Jamm line — the implication that he both owns ninja stars and considers them appropriate hospital equipment is perfectly absurd. High quotability. The escalation from 'no fighting' to ninja star regret is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're gonna serve brunch items, but we're gonna call them 'breakfast for dinner.' No wait, that's already a thing. Okay, how about 'brinner'?

dialogue.speaker: Mitch
dialogue.line: I like that. Brinner.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Right? It's like breakfast had a baby with dinner, and that baby is brinner.

dialogue.speaker: Mitch
dialogue.line: That's genius. I'm in. Let's do brinner.

jokes.text: Hey, girl. What up? What are you wearing? It's to distract people from my black eye. See? It's working.
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives at work post-hospital wearing something presumably outrageous to cover her black eye
jokes.punchline: Leslie's outfit is so distracting that April asks about it; Leslie's explanation — it's working as intended — implies the outfit is wilder than the injury
jokes.explanation: A visual joke — we can't see the outfit from the transcript but the exchange implies something truly remarkable. 'See? It's working' confirms the outfit is successfully distracting. Good economy and character-appropriate absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Mitch
dialogue.line: I have to give all the credit to Tom. He really knows his stuff when it comes to business.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, what? I did all the work on this project.

dialogue.speaker: Mitch
dialogue.line: Right, but Tom was there too.

jokes.text: There is some good news. That Mike Patterson guy's show just aired, everyone is angry, and Jamm is introducing a secession bill. How is any of that good news? It's not. I just wanted you to have a brief moment of happiness before you got sadder.
jokes.setup: April announces 'some good news'
jokes.punchline: The 'good news' is a list of disasters; April immediately admits there is no good news — she just wanted Leslie to experience a 'brief moment of happiness' before more sadness
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. April's strategy of fabricating optimism to give Leslie 'a brief moment of happiness before you got sadder' is both dark and oddly sweet — quintessentially April. The structure is perfect: false setup, list of disasters, then the reveal of April's manipulation rationale. Highly quotable and character-defining.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'm going to tell you something I wish someone had told me when I was your age. Back in 1987, I was working on a Craftsman table saw. The blade kept binding up on me, no matter what I did. I adjusted the fence, checked the alignment, replaced the belt. Nothing worked. So I sat down, and I thought about that saw for three days straight. By the fourth day, I realized the problem wasn't the saw. It was me. I wasn't respecting the saw. Once I started respecting the saw, everything got better.

jokes.text: It sucks. It's okay, April. It's fine. You know, it's a challenge. It's just like a big, fun... stinking turd nugget. It sucks.
jokes.setup: April offers empathy about the merger struggles
jokes.punchline: Leslie tries to spin it positively ('big, fun...') and lands on 'stinking turd nugget' — she can't maintain the optimism
jokes.explanation: 'Stinking turd nugget' as the phrase Leslie's optimism collapses into is very funny. The structure — she tries to Leslie-ize the problem, the metaphor fails, she lands on turd nugget, April echoes 'it sucks' — is well-constructed. The line itself is unusually quotable for a scatological term.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And that's why you need to let it cool down before you touch it again.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, what does any of that have to do with my situation?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Everything, Leslie. You're the radiator.

jokes.text: I wonder what other excellent surprise lies in store for Leslie Knope.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in full self-pity mode after the merger disasters
jokes.punchline: She speaks about herself in the third person with mock-journalistic gravity — simultaneously self-pitying and self-aware
jokes.explanation: Third-person self-pity is a solid Leslie mode. Works as a transition beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You know, a radiator is like a relationship. If it's not functioning properly, you need to get under there and figure out what's wrong with it. You can't just ignore it and hope it fixes itself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, are you seriously giving me relationship advice right now?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm talking about radiators.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's exactly what I mean. You're avoiding—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But if you actually listen to what I said, it applies to everything. Including your situation with Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. That was... that was actually really good advice.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know. I'm very good at advice. I just prefer to deliver it through the metaphor of home maintenance.

jokes.text: Now I shall meet with a very important person whilst sporting a gruesome shiner. Hey, you're also wearing a tie-dye t-shirt. Oh, yes! I am! Wonderful!
jokes.setup: Grant Larson from the National Park Service arrives for the meeting; Leslie has a black eye
jokes.punchline: April reminds Leslie she's also wearing a tie-dye t-shirt; Leslie's delighted 'Oh, yes! I am! Wonderful!' implies she'd forgotten this detail and finds it a bonus
jokes.explanation: The visual of Leslie meeting a federal official with a black eye and tie-dye is strong. Her delighted rediscovery of the shirt ('Oh, yes! I am! Wonderful!') is characterful — she's not embarrassed, she's pleased. Callback to the distraction outfit.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not crying. There's just a lot of smoke in here.

jokes.text: Great. Well, this week just keeps getting better and better. Thank you for coming by and plunging a dagger into my already-bleeding corpse.
jokes.setup: Grant Larson says the National Park proposal can't happen
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response escalates from sarcasm ('keeps getting better') to full dramatic metaphor ('plunging a dagger into my already-bleeding corpse')
jokes.explanation: The escalation from conventional sarcasm to a very specific gore metaphor is good Leslie dramatics. 'Already-bleeding corpse' is a strong image. Works well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't think of one reason not to take this job.

dialogue.speaker: Grant
dialogue.line: Well, technically, a double negative is a positive, so you've actually given me one reason to hire you.

jokes.text: I've got two words for you-- 'Tom's Bistro,' an old-fashioned, old-world Italian restaurant...
jokes.setup: Tom dramatically builds up to his pitch with 'I've got two words for you'
jokes.punchline: The reveal is 'Tom's Bistro' — technically four words if you count the apostrophe as a letter, but more importantly, it's the restaurant idea he had previously dismissed as too risky
jokes.explanation: The 'two words' setup for a phrase that isn't two words is a mild classic. Here it works because Tom's confidence in his pivot is so full-commit. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm so glad to meet you, Mr. Grant. I'd love to shake your hand.

dialogue.speaker: Grant
dialogue.line: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh no, I can't quite... my depth perception is off today.

jokes.text: Why does that say 'dry cleaning chemical transactional holding company?' Ben! You brought the wrong easel. God! Can't take this guy anywhere.
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching Tom's Bistro to the investor with a dramatic visual aid
jokes.punchline: The visual aid is Ben's dry cleaning chemicals presentation instead; Tom blames Ben in front of the investor
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the dry cleaning idea. 'Can't take this guy anywhere' while Tom is literally the problem is ironic. Works as a physical comedy beat even in transcript form.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I want to invest in your restaurant.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Really?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, I believe in you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ben, that's... wait. How much are we talking?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, I was thinking—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Never mind. Doesn't matter. I don't want your money.

jokes.text: Liam Bonneville actually used it to humiliate staffers, but... he's kind of a bad boy.
jokes.setup: Grant explains Leslie's report got shuffled around and Liam Bonneville used it
jokes.punchline: Liam Bonneville — the 'bad boy of the Department of Interior' — is confirmed real and his bad behavior is an internal report being used to humiliate people; Larson's fond 'he's kind of a bad boy' treats this as charming
jokes.explanation: Pays off the earlier bit about Liam Bonneville being the 'bad boy' of the DOI. His actual bad-boy behavior being 'using reports to humiliate staffers' is perfectly mundane for a government bad boy. The callback is earned and the escalation of his reputation vs. reality is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I spent the day teaching my son about the government's fundamental incompetence and the dangers of trusting bureaucrats. It was beautiful.

jokes.text: Liam B-- You don't have to tell me!
jokes.setup: Larson mentions Liam Bonneville
jokes.punchline: Leslie lights up with recognition and cuts Larson off — she's a Liam Bonneville fan, despite him being an obscure bureaucrat who humiliates staffers with her work
jokes.explanation: Leslie cutting off the full name with 'You don't have to tell me!' — as if she's a fangirl of a mid-level DOI official — is a great payoff to the running Liam Bonneville bit. Character integration is high; her enthusiasm for obscure government figures is a core trait.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: He's got that look of a man who just closed a deal with the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, he's three months old. He probably just has gas.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's what I said. He closed a deal.

jokes.text: Okay! As long as you're running, I'm in.
jokes.setup: Ben has made the case for Tom's restaurant, emphasizing his role in managing it
jokes.punchline: The investor commits — but only because Ben will be running it, not because of Tom's vision. Tom's dream investment is secured by his boss's credibility
jokes.explanation: The irony of Tom's dream being funded contingent on Ben's involvement is a good character sting. The investor's conditional 'as long as you're running' slightly deflates Tom's victory.

jokes.text: Hey, kid... your boss here sure knows his stuff.
jokes.setup: The investor meeting ends successfully
jokes.punchline: The investor compliments 'the kid's boss' — referring to Ben — not realizing Tom is the one with the dream and Ben is the straight man who sold it
jokes.explanation: The role reversal — Tom being called 'kid' to his boss Ben — is a gentle ironic twist. Works as a button to the investor scene.

jokes.text: Ron. What are you doing here? The most important government work I've ever done-- sanding rat urine stains out of this floor.
jokes.setup: Leslie finds Ron on the abandoned third floor
jokes.punchline: Ron describes sanding rat urine stains as 'the most important government work I've ever done' — which both reveals his contempt for all other government work and his genuine satisfaction with manual labor
jokes.explanation: One of the best Ron Swanson lines in the episode. Calling rodent urine remediation 'the most important government work I've ever done' is both a perfect anti-government statement and a genuine expression of his values — craftwork over bureaucracy. High character integration, excellent economy. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: Yesterday, I fixed that old steam radiator. Threaded a new valve into the side, removed the handle from the base, unscrewed the packing nut from the stem. This subpar toolbox only had one wrench, so I was lucky it was a three-quarters or I'd have been screwed. Yeah, man, you are lucky. Come on, Ron. What the hell? I need your help.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ron for help with her personal crisis; Ron begins to speak
jokes.punchline: Ron answers with an extended technical account of radiator repair — the response to an emotional crisis is plumbing mechanics; Leslie's increasingly exasperated 'Come on, Ron' and 'What the hell?' shows she's losing patience as the subtext takes its time
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in Ron Swanson communication style. He IS answering the question — just via a radiator metaphor — but Leslie (and the audience) has to wait through actual plumbing specifics to get there. 'Yeah, man, you are lucky' as Leslie's defeated attempt to play along before snapping is perfect. The sustained misdirection earns its high score. One of the best scenes in the episode.

jokes.text: Now...to most people, this story would seem boring. That's ridiculous. It's a story about a radiator.
jokes.setup: Ron anticipates that the radiator story might not seem relevant
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'that's ridiculous' is sarcastic — she IS bored — but Ron takes it as sincere and elaborates anyway. The self-aware meta-joke about the radiator story being boring is itself delivered with no irony by Ron
jokes.explanation: The exchange works on two levels: Ron thinks Leslie is agreeing that radiator stories are exciting; the audience knows she's being sarcastic. Ron's genuine 'that's ridiculous, it's a story about a radiator' treats his enthusiasm as universal. Very well-constructed.

jokes.text: What's that? Nothing. Clearing my throat.
jokes.setup: Ron has just given Leslie warm, sincere advice about loving her work
jokes.punchline: There's clearly a sound — presumably Ron suppressing genuine emotion — and his cover is 'clearing my throat': the least convincing denial of a tender moment
jokes.explanation: This is the emotional and comedic peak of the episode. Ron — the man who introduced his own son as 'John middle name redacted' — is moved by the Leslie moment and hides it with 'clearing my throat.' The economy is exceptional: two exchanges, seven words total, and it lands with enormous warmth and humor. Character integration is as high as it gets — this could only be Ron Swanson. A deeply earned laugh.

jokes.text: I've been thinking about your offer. And I have to say I can't think of one single reason not to take it. That's great! I'm sorry, I meant... because I can think of a lot of reasons not to take it. Okay, wow, that's very misleading phraseology.
jokes.setup: Leslie is responding to Larson's job offer
jokes.punchline: Her double-negative construction creates a false positive that excites him; she corrects herself and he calls out 'very misleading phraseology' with bureaucratic precision
jokes.explanation: The double-negative confusion is a classic comedy construction. 'Very misleading phraseology' is a funny government-speak response from Larson. Well-structured.

jokes.text: That's not your hand. Here it is. Sorry, my depth perception is totally screwed up.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to shake Larson's hand to close the meeting
jokes.punchline: She grabs the wrong thing first — presumably his arm or a table edge — and explains her depth perception is 'totally screwed up' due to the black eye
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the black eye consequences. The depth perception explanation is a functional medical-comedy beat. Not exceptional but well-placed as a scene button.

jokes.text: Really happy that worked out for you, Tom, but you kinda sold me out back there. I know, and I'm sorry. But Mitch asked me what I was passionate about, and honestly I'm never gonna be passionate about dry cleaning chemicals.
jokes.setup: Ben is mildly put out that Tom abandoned the dry cleaning pitch
jokes.punchline: Tom's apology is genuine but the reasoning — he can't be passionate about tetrachloroethylene — is completely valid, and Ben's hurt feelings over a pitch for dry cleaning chemical distribution are absurd
jokes.explanation: The callback to the dry cleaning idea and Ben's investment in it is a good closing beat. The inherent absurdity of anyone caring about this pitch is the joke.

jokes.text: Then count me in as the second investor in Tom's Bistro. Thanks, man. I know this is a symbolic gesture, but my investor floor is $1,000. So as of now, you own zero shares. Cool! Thanks for clearing that up.
jokes.setup: Ben offers to invest in Tom's Bistro as a show of support
jokes.punchline: He immediately follows up by clarifying his minimum investment is $1,000 and he has none, so he owns zero shares — the symbolic gesture collapses under its own math
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent — warm gesture immediately self-negated by pedantic accounting. Ben's compulsion to clarify that he owns zero shares, and Tom's breezy acceptance ('Cool!'), is perfect for both characters. The investor floor clause is a wonderfully specific detail.

jokes.text: Oh, look, John. It's red pine. They were gonna put flecked linoleum over this beautifully preserved knotty red pine. Most people in this world, John, are ass[bleep].
jokes.setup: Ron and baby John are surveying the floor renovation
jokes.punchline: Ron's discovery of covered hardwood escalates to a comprehensive life lesson for his infant: most people are assholes. Delivered with total sincerity as fatherly wisdom
jokes.explanation: This is the second-best joke in the episode. The structure is perfect: Ron identifies a specific woodworking injustice, and his reaction — to tell his newborn that most people are assholes — is both a non-sequitur and completely logical from Ron's perspective. The escalation from 'beautiful knotty red pine' to a blanket condemnation of humanity, addressed to an infant as wisdom, is brilliant. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific. The specific species of wood makes it funnier.

jokes.text: This is the best day I've ever spent in a government building, and luckily my son was here to share it with me. He now has that satisfied look that only comes with the pride of labor. Or he pooped. Either way, well done, John.
jokes.setup: Ron reflects on the day spent renovating the floor with baby John
jokes.punchline: His attribution of the baby's expression to 'pride of labor' is immediately undercut by the obvious alternative — the baby probably pooped — but Ron's 'either way, well done, John' accepts both as equally valid
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect episode button. 'Either way, well done, John' treats a dirty diaper as equivalent to craftsman pride — which is both absurd and somehow deeply Ron. The structure is flawless: romanticized observation, immediate deflation, philosophical acceptance. High quotability. The episode ends on Ron's worldview applied to his son, which is emotionally resonant and very funny.

tmdb_overview: Leslie aims to create a new town slogan, but runs afoul of local shock jocks. Andy scouts bands to play the Unity Concert and discovers an interesting secret about Ron, while Tom looks for a restaurant locale with Donna and April.
insight: Seventy-two laughs on absurdist character work, but emotional stakes soften the comedic edge.
